title: Unity Anchor
concept: Pressure from outside the relationship — family disapproval, minority stress, being judged as a couple — gets named as the shared problem, not filed as a flaw in either of you or in the relationship itself.
whenToUse: When disapproval, discrimination, or outsider judgement (family, community, strangers) is putting pressure on the two of you, and it’s starting to look like a problem between you instead of a problem coming from outside. Also for jealousy about people outside the relationship: decide together how you respond — never by limiting who your partner sees or talks to.
steps: Pause before reacting — don’t react to the outside pressure itself yet. Ask what’s actually needed right now: reassurance, a plan, or just to vent.
Trace the source — is this about us, or about their disapproval landing on us? Name it out loud as external: “That’s coming from them, not from us.”
Name the unit — say it out loud: “We’re on the same side of this.”

Agree your response — decide together, as a team, how the two of you will respond next time. Never decide how much contact your partner has with their own family or friends. If it’s a recurring source, log it at your next Weekly Reset.

phrases.text: That’s coming from them, not from us.
We’re on the same side of this.
What do you actually need right now — reassurance, a plan, or just to vent?

working: A recurring comment from family lands on one partner. Instead of debating whether it’s a fair criticism, you name it as outside pressure, check what’s needed, and agree how the two of you will respond next time it comes up.
notWorking: Treating the outside pressure as evidence about the relationship — relitigating whether the disapproval has a point, or letting one partner absorb it alone while the other stays neutral.
activity: Name one recurring source of outside pressure on your relationship. Practise the phrase “We’re on the same side of this” out loud. Agree on one thing you’ll do differently the next time it comes up.
warn: Unity Anchor decides how the couple responds to outside pressure — never how much access a relative gets to your partner. No tool is ever used to limit a partner’s contact with friends, family, money, phone or movement.
